items.answer: The design-prototype-evaluate cycle in experience design consists of designing, quickly prototyping the design, evaluating it, finding problems, refining the design, and repeating this with new prototypes and evaluations, which may require many cycles before the design is stabilized.
Prototypes can be broadly considered in two categories, horizontal prototypes and vertical prototypes.
Prototypes can be broadly considered in two categories, horizontal prototypes and vertical prototypes.

A low-fidelity prototype is a prototype created without technological intervention, programming, code, or a computer, using non-digital materials such as paper, cardboard, or wood, and paper mockups of the look, feel, and functionality of an interface are a popular example.

To represent interaction, a low-fidelity prototype needs a series of interface sketches rather than a single sketch, a practice often called storyboarding; a single sketch gives a horizontal prototype, whereas a series of sketches can give a vertical prototype depicting interaction.
The fifth rule in system design is to offer error prevention and simple error handling.

questions.question: Which description matches a throwaway prototype?
options: It is refined from a simpler whole-system version into the final product
It is used for quick evaluation and then discarded
It is built by integrating separately tested modules
It is represented by a storyboard of interface sketches
questions.explanation: Prototypes can be throwaway, incremental, or evolutionary, and throwaway prototypes are specifically used for quick evaluation and then discarded.

questions.question: Low-fidelity cardboard mockups and paper sketches are mainly suitable for throwaway prototypes because:
options: they support interactive multimedia content for augmented reality evaluation
they can be retained and refined into the final product
they are low-cost and discarding them does not incur significant cost
they allow separate modules to be prototyped and tested before integration
questions.explanation: Throwaway prototypes should be easy and fast to create, and low-fidelity mockups and sketches are suitable because they are inexpensive and cheap to discard.

questions.question: Which description matches incremental prototyping?
options: It is refined from a simpler whole-system version into the final product
It is used for quick evaluation and then discarded
It is built by separately prototyping and testing modules and then integrating them
It is made as low-cost paper sketches that are easy to discard
questions.explanation: Incremental prototypes are created when the system is divided into modules, each module is separately prototyped and tested, and the modules are then integrated into the overall system.

questions.question: Which description matches evolutionary prototyping?
options: It is used for quick evaluation and then discarded
It is made from cardboard mockups and paper sketches that are easy to discard
It starts with a simpler version of the whole system and is refined into the final product
It is built by separately prototyping and testing modules before integration
questions.explanation: Evolutionary prototypes are created by prototyping and testing the whole system from the beginning, starting with a simpler version and refining it until it becomes the final product.

data.text: Prototypes can be classified as throwaway, incremental, or evolutionary. Throwaway prototypes are used for quick evaluation and are often created using fast and inexpensive low-fidelity mockups. Incremental prototypes involve testing separate modules before integration, while evolutionary prototypes involve refining a simple version of the entire system until it becomes the final product.
points: Prototypes can be classified as throwaway, incremental, or evolutionary.
Throwaway prototypes are used for quick evaluation and then discarded.
Low-fidelity mockups and paper sketches are suitable for throwaway prototypes because they are easy and inexpensive to create.
Incremental prototypes involve prototyping and testing separate modules before integrating them into the overall system.
Evolutionary prototypes involve refining a simple version of the whole system until it becomes the final product.

questions.question: What is the main distinction between quick prototype evaluation and a robust evaluation technique?
options: Quick evaluation is performed only after the final product is available.
Quick evaluation is a fast, low-cost way to evaluate a prototype early in design.
Quick evaluation requires a full evaluation setup with extensive resources.
A robust evaluation is fast and low-cost, while quick evaluation is slow and resource-intensive.
questions.explanation: Quick evaluation, also called expert evaluation, is meant to evaluate a prototype quickly and cheaply at an early stage of design, unlike a more robust evaluation setup.

questions.question: What are the prerequisites for performing quick or expert evaluation?
options: At least a full implementation and a robust evaluation setup.
At least a final product and a single evaluator.
At least a high-fidelity prototype and no evaluator team.
At least a low-fidelity prototype and a team of evaluators.
questions.explanation: Quick or expert evaluation needs at least a low-fidelity prototype, with better-quality prototypes preferred, and a team of evaluators.

questions.question: Why can quick or expert evaluation rely mainly on design-team members or domain experts instead of end users?
options: They are assumed to have user-like experience, and engaging them is less complicated, quicker, and cheaper.
Engaging end users is usually less complicated, quicker, and cheaper.
Designers are assumed to be less user-like than end users.
Their feedback is used to verify the full implementation rather than the interface.
questions.explanation: Design-team members or domain experts are used because they are assumed to have user-like experience and can be engaged more simply, quickly, and cheaply than a full end-user evaluation.

questions.question: Although usability testing normally involves users, who mainly conducts quick or expert evaluation?
options: The design team or skilled designers with knowledge of the problem domain.
Only software developers, because they are testing code design.
Only external evaluators from a robust evaluation setup.
Only end users, because usability testing always requires users.
questions.explanation: Quick evaluation is a usability test, but its team is primarily the design team or skilled designers with problem-domain knowledge, with a few end users optional.

questions.question: How is the final list of usability issues produced in expert evaluation?
options: End users review the independent reports and publish the final list.
Evaluators discuss in one group and agree on issues before inspecting the prototype.
A single evaluator writes the final list without combining independent reports.
Each evaluator independently reports issues, and the design team or team lead combines the reports.
questions.explanation: In expert evaluation, evaluators work independently, each producing a report of perceived usability issues, which the design team or team lead then combines into a final list.

data.text: Expert evaluation is a quick and cost-effective way to assess a prototype at an early design stage. It requires a low-fidelity prototype and a team of three to five design team members or domain experts who provide feedback to save time and costs. Each evaluator independently produces a report, which is then combined into a final list of usability issues.
points: Quick evaluation is a fast and cheap way to assess a prototype at an early design stage.
The process requires at least a low-fidelity prototype and a team of evaluators.
Design team members or experts perform the evaluation because they are faster and cheaper to engage than end users, who may optionally be included.
A team of three to five members is sufficient for the evaluation.
Evaluators work independently to create reports that are then combined into a final list of usability issues.

questions.question: What is the minimum prototype needed for a cognitive walkthrough?
options: A high-fidelity vertical prototype
A low-fidelity vertical prototype
A low-fidelity horizontal prototype
A complete full implementation
questions.explanation: A cognitive walkthrough requires at least a low-fidelity vertical prototype, while a high-fidelity prototype is more welcome but not required.

questions.question: In a cognitive walkthrough, what do evaluators do with the described task?
options: They compare it with the final product to check resource requirements
They evaluate the whole system using a heuristic checklist
They ask end users to answer the usability questions directly
They convert it into interface-level tasks and perform them in the prototype
questions.explanation: The scenario's task is converted into interface-level actions, which evaluators then perform with the prototype.

questions.question: What must evaluators provide for each usability question in a cognitive walkthrough?
options: A resource-optimization recommendation
A detailed report explaining where difficulty occurred and why
A simple yes or no answer
A single tick on a heuristic checklist
questions.explanation: For each usability question, evaluators must explain where they felt difficulty in the interface or interaction and why, rather than giving a simple yes or no.

questions.question: What form can a low-fidelity cognitive-walkthrough prototype take?
options: Paper storyboards that sketch screen changes after each interaction
A complete full implementation of the system
A high-fidelity prototype made with Adobe Flash
A set of usability heuristics for checklist inspection
questions.explanation: A low-fidelity prototype can be simple paper prototypes made with storyboarding, where each prototype is a series of sketches showing screen changes after interactions.

questions.question: At the end of a cognitive walkthrough, what is done with the evaluators' reports?
options: They are collected, combined, and analyzed to identify broader usability issues
They are used to choose an authoring tool for the prototype
They are replaced by a checklist of system heuristics
They are published as final product requirements
questions.explanation: The evaluators' reports are collected, combined, and analyzed at the end of the evaluation session to identify broader usability issues.

data.text: Cognitive walkthrough is a quick expert evaluation technique used to identify usability problems by inspecting a prototype. The method requires a team of three to five members and at least a low-fidelity vertical prototype. Evaluators perform interface-level tasks from a scenario using predefined usability questions as guidelines. Finally, the evaluators provide detailed reports on their difficulties, which are then analyzed to identify broader usability issues.
points: Cognitive walkthrough is a quick expert evaluation technique used to identify usability problems by inspecting a prototype.
The method requires a team of three to five members and at least a low-fidelity vertical prototype.
Evaluators perform interface-level tasks from a scenario using predefined usability questions as guidelines.
Evaluators provide detailed reports on their difficulties, which are analyzed to identify broader usability issues.

questions.question: What distinguishes heuristic evaluation from a task-specific evaluation?
options: Evaluators inspect only the parts needed for one task.
Evaluators assess a prototype by performing a task scenario.
Evaluators check a whole prototype against heuristics without a task scenario.
Evaluators measure task performance to evaluate the whole system.
questions.explanation: Heuristic evaluation assesses a presented prototype by ticking checklist items, without a task scenario or task performance, to evaluate the whole system rather than one task.

questions.question: Why do broader usability checklists usually contain fewer heuristics than detailed system-specific checklists?
options: They are broader in nature and not specific to any particular interface.
They are detailed checklists tied to one particular interface.
They are broader in nature and specific to a single interface.
They are task-oriented checklists tied to one scenario.
questions.explanation: Broader usability checklists contain fewer heuristics because they cover broader principles rather than details of a particular interface.

questions.question: What does the 'recognition rather than recall' heuristic require in an interface?
options: The user should prevent errors before they occur through design.
The user should recognize from visible elements what to do rather than recall it.
The user should have freedom to undo or cancel actions.
The user should recall commands without relying on visible elements.
questions.explanation: Recognition rather than recall means the user should be able to recognize from interface elements what to do, because recollection is more difficult than recognition.

questions.question: How does the prototype requirement for heuristic evaluation differ from that for a cognitive walkthrough?
options: Both methods require a vertical prototype to identify usability problems.
Heuristic evaluation needs a vertical prototype; cognitive walkthrough can use a horizontal prototype.
Heuristic evaluation requires a final product; cognitive walkthrough can use a low-fidelity storyboard.
Heuristic evaluation can use low-fidelity, mainly horizontal prototypes; cognitive walkthrough needs a vertical prototype.
questions.explanation: Heuristic evaluation can identify problems from simple low-fidelity prototypes, primarily horizontal ones, whereas a cognitive walkthrough requires a vertical prototype.

questions.question: What does each evaluator do during heuristic evaluation?
options: They select only a few heuristics to check before the evaluation.
They perform task scenarios and report task completion rates.
They give a simple yes or no answer without explaining violations.
They check each heuristic, report violations with reasons, and the reports are combined.
questions.explanation: Each evaluator evaluates the prototype against each heuristic, reports whether it is followed or violated with reasons if violated, and the reports are combined to identify major issues.

data.text: Heuristic evaluation is a technique where evaluators use a checklist of heuristics to assess a prototype and perform a comprehensive evaluation without a task scenario. This process can use system-specific checklists or broader principles like Nielsen's 10 heuristics, which are applicable to most interactive systems. A team of at least three to five evaluators can use these heuristics to identify violations in low-fidelity prototypes and compile reports to highlight major issues.
points: Heuristic evaluation is a technique where evaluators assess a prototype using a checklist of heuristics without a task scenario.
Checklists for evaluating interfaces can be system-specific or focus on broader usability principles.
Nielsen's 10 heuristics are a general set applicable to most interactive systems.
Heuristic evaluation can be conducted on low-fidelity prototypes by a team of at least three to five evaluators.
Evaluators report whether each heuristic is followed or violated and compile these reports to identify major issues.

items.reason: Cardboard mockups, paper sketches and paper prototypes are low-fidelity prototype forms; a high-fidelity prototype is a higher-fidelity prototype, not a low-fidelity form.

questions.question: Why are low-fidelity cardboard mockups and paper sketches mainly suitable for throwaway prototypes, and what condition must such prototypes satisfy to remain useful?
questions.reference_answer: Throwaway prototypes are prototypes that are used for quick evaluation and then discarded. Low-fidelity cardboard mockups and paper sketches are mainly suitable for them because they are less costly and discarding them does not incur significant cost. They are also a good match because throwaway prototypes should be easy and fast to create, otherwise working with them becomes expensive.

questions.question: How do incremental prototypes and evolutionary prototypes differ in the way they follow from the structure of a system design?
questions.reference_answer: Incremental prototypes are created when the system design divides the system into units or modules, each module is separately prototyped and tested, and the modules are then integrated into the overall system. Evolutionary prototypes are created by prototyping and testing the whole system from the beginning, starting with a simpler version, refining it, adding more functionalities, and altering it based on testing results. The evolutionary approach does this rather than prototyping separate modules and combining them.

questions.question: How do cognitive walkthrough and heuristic evaluation differ in the prototype, scenario, and evaluation procedure they require?
questions.reference_answer: Cognitive walkthrough is a quick expert evaluation and usability inspection method that identifies usability problems by inspecting a prototype, and it requires at least a low-fidelity vertical prototype plus a scenario whose task is converted into interface-level tasks. Heuristic evaluation is an evaluation technique in which evaluators assess a presented prototype by ticking items on a checklist of heuristics, without a task scenario or task performance, to evaluate the whole system rather than one task. Because heuristic evaluation can use low-fidelity prototypes, primarily horizontal prototypes, with vertical prototypes optional, it is less dependent on task-driven interaction than cognitive walkthrough.

questions.question: How can expert evaluation support repeated refinement of a prototype, and why can its evaluation team rely on design team members or domain experts rather than a full end-user team?
questions.reference_answer: When a design is prototyped, evaluated, problems are found, and the design is refined repeatedly, expert evaluation can provide quick and cheap evaluation of a low-fidelity prototype at an early stage of design. The required evaluation team can be the design team itself, skilled designers with knowledge and skill in the problem domain, or domain experts, and it may optionally include a few end users. It can rely on these people rather than a full end-user evaluation team because they are assumed to have user-like experience, their feedback likely reflects users, and engaging them is less complicated, quicker, and cheaper.
